Transnational mobilities of private higher education policy across spaces, time and through actors: a case study of Vietnam
Supporting participatory PhDs: a call to action
abstract: Abstract There has been sustained and growing interest in public policy, professional practice, and research, in what has come to be called patient and public, or service user, involvement. Requirements for such involvement are now embedded within health and care legislation, professional education, and training, and the expectations of many research funders and commissioners. There has also been an increasing interest in public involvement in research, learning, and specifically in the undertaking and assessment of PhDs. However, provisions and requirements for PhDs have not caught up with these developments, despite them being offered as providing advanced research training. Consequently, obstacles to fulfilling such involvement are present in existing arrangements concerning the authorship, regulations, funding, and assessment of PhDs, which seek to be participatory and collaborative. This article reports on this issue and the emergence of an international Participatory PhD Network to support this developing field as a result, and the ways forward it suggests. title: Learning critical realism in higher education: metaphor-work as collective pedagogical practice
Reframing doctoral research instability through a supervisory risk lens
abstract: Abstract This conceptual article develops a supervisory risk framework to explain how doctoral research projects become unstable through interacting design vulnerabilities rather than isolated student shortcomings. Drawing on scholarship in doctoral supervision, academic socialisation, and higher education, it proposes a risk framework comprising research question scope, methodological alignment, timeline design, communication structures, and expectation alignment. These domains are conceptualised as interacting elements within supervisory design rather than discrete problems emerging later in candidature. The framework is intended to apply across disciplinary traditions characterised by differing epistemological assumptions and methodological approaches. By reframing project instability as a systemic and developmental issue, this article shifts attention from reactive remediation toward preventive supervisory design embedded within institutional performance environments. In doing so, it positions supervision as a meso-level mechanism through which broader institutional conditions shape doctoral project trajectories. The role of research project participation on PhD students perceived skill enhancement
abstract: Abstract This paper explores the association between PhD students’ research project participation and perceived skill enhancement during doctoral studies. Based on data of 10,819 PhD students in Chinese mainland universities, we assess if they perceive participation in research projects to have enhanced their research and generic skills. The findings show that participation in research projects leads to a perceived enhancement of skills. Participation in more projects leads to a perceived accumulated gain in both research and generic skills. The perception of skill enhancement from participating in projects can be mostly explained by the level of satisfaction with research project participation. The effects of ability, proxied by the undergraduate university and the number of publications of students as the first or corresponding authors, are mixed. Student engagement in specific tasks, such as project research design, contributes to the perception of skill enhancement, whereas participation in most other tasks appears irrelevant. This suggests that involvement in particular activities may be less critical than anticipated for the perceived development of research and generic skill

title: Threshold concepts: Tensions and truths
abstract: Abstract Since their introduction, threshold concepts have served as a framework for understanding the transformative nature of learning across different disciplines. Although threshold concepts framework is a relative newcomer in the teaching and learning space, two decades of research have exposed persistent debates about the theoretical coherence of threshold concepts and critiques about their application. Critics point to the “conceptual fuzziness” of the framework, leading to calls to abandon threshold concepts in favor of less ambiguous models. The purpose of threshold concepts is also debated—should educators aim to redesign curricula to smooth the learner’s journey by eliminating these “stuck places” or should these thresholds be purposefully fortified as essential sites of productive struggle? This paper serves to address these debates head-on, and in doing so argues that the ambiguity of threshold concepts is not a theoretical flaw, but an accurate reflection of the complex, non-linear nature of deep and transformative learning. Beyond graduate outcomes: a temporal-agential perspective on students’ capacity to aspire in transnational higher education
Organizing research security: the embedded advisory model in Canadian universities
Governance arrangements and policy instruments in university endowment development: a comparative analysis of Taiwan, Singapore, Hong Kong, and China
Research-based teaching and the predicament of assessment: rethinking evaluation challenges through the sociology of regimes of engagement
abstract: Abstract Research-based teaching offers valuable learning opportunities by involving students in research and inquiry. However, employing these approaches within standardised university assessment frameworks may create tensions. Drawing on ethnographic research from a university-wide initiative to integrate research in teaching, this article examines how assessment practices interact with pedagogies of research-based teaching. Our analysis shows that academics and students experience a discrepancy between how students engage in processes of research and when focusing on the final assessment. Drawing on the sociology of regimes of engagement, we analyse these experiences as reflecting tensions between different ways of engaging and the various benefits or goods they involve. We show how a tension between an explorative engagement (oriented towards discovery) and an engagement in plan (focused on predefined outcomes) predominates these experiences and practices of research-based teaching. Our analysis highlights how teachers sustain an explorative engagement within plural regimes through a delicate art of composition, creating protected spaces for exploration or modifying assessment

Resisting managerialism through academic voice: contesting the quantification of community engagement in the social sciences and humanities
The ‘failed researcher’ – perceptions of illegitimacy and the marginalisation of education focused academics in Australia
abstract: Abstract For many academics, appointment to an education focused (EF) role can trigger a sense of illegitimacy and professional marginalisation. This experience is not universal, but it is reported repeatedly in the literature. Whilst existing research has documented these experiences, less attention has been paid to how they are institutionally produced and sustained. This paper addresses this gap by examining the institutional construction of EF academics’ perceived illegitimacy within Australian universities. Drawing on interview data and neo-institutional theory, the study identifies a recurring conception of the EF academic as the ‘failed researcher’. Within this institutional identity category, the EF academic’s focus on teaching and students’ learning is framed not as specialisation, but as deviation from the idealised research-active norm. It shapes EF academics’ experiences in overt and covert ways, through workload practices, promotion processes, informal interactions, and organisational cultures, contributing to patterns of exclusion across many universities. Early career academics’ identity formation in international branch campus: a comparative analysis of international and Chinese scholars’ experiences in China
abstract: Abstract As transnational higher education expands, international branch campuses (IBCs) have become key sites where global, national, and local academic logics intersect. However, limited research has explored how early career academics (ECAs) construct their academic identities within these hybrid institutions. Drawing on the concept of global-national-local imbrications, this study comparatively examines the academic identity formation of Chinese and international ECAs working in an IBC in China. Findings show that the IBC generated shared uncertainty, but it positioned the two groups differently: Chinese ECAs more often negotiated dual legitimacy across global and domestic arenas, whereas international ECAs drew legitimacy from their international status but faced greater challenges in becoming locally recognized and connected. In response, Chinese ECAs adopted amphibious strategies to balance these demands, while international ECAs relied more on peer networks to navigate local constraints and sustain their early-career trajectories. Network embeddedness of knowledge creation among international migrant academics in China’s Sino-Foreign Cooperative Universities
Research on future learning centers: co-intelligence theory-based framework for student development in the era of AI
Outsiders within: exploring integration strategies of international faculty in chinese higher education institutions
abstract: Abstract International faculty (IF) are increasingly recruited to Chinese universities to support knowledge transfer and internationalisation, yet they frequently report experiencing persistent marginal positions. This study examines how IF in Chinese higher education navigate this marginal status. Drawing on thirty semi-structured interviews, we identify five reflexive tactics: playing by the rules, contextual collaboration, negotiating around the rules, tactical non-pursuit, and strategic self-detachment. These tactics are deployed across four domains of institutional integration: cultural norms, interpersonal relations, resources, and academic practice. By foregrounding reflexivity, the analysis reframes integration not as a binary outcome of assimilation or marginalisation, but as a non-linear decision-making process mediated by ethical judgement. The study reveals that integration encompasses not only intercultural competence and resource allocation, but also a strategic balancing of selective engagement and detachment, driven by distinct ethical foci. Findings underscore the value of more inclusive institutional cultures and greater tolerance for outsider-within positions.

Assessment Arrythmia: restoring rhythms of time, space, and practice in higher education
abstract: Abstract Higher education practice is increasingly shaped by expanding workloads and cultures of acceleration. These pressures are felt acutely in the domain of assessment. As marking cycles shorten, deadlines proliferate, and institutional metrics dominate academic time, assessment risks becoming a site of temporal strain rather than pedagogical care. This paper deploys the concept of arrhythmia as a metaphor for the increasingly fragmented, rushed, and disjointed nature of assessment in higher education. Drawing on contemporary challenges in academic practice, we argue that assessment has lost its pedagogical rhythm, becoming governed by institutional workload clocks rather than learning-centred temporalities. Engaging Lefebvre’s rhythmanalysis, we identify three interrelated symptoms of assessment arrhythmia: unsustainable acceleration and pace; temporal surveillance; and temporal dissonance within modularised curricula. We respond to these conditions by proposing a series of recommendations aimed at restoring more relational, integrated, and temporally aligned approaches to assessment. title: Integration or stratification? Cumulative advantage and prestige homophily in the CEEPUS inter-university network
abstract: Abstract International student mobility is often framed as an integrative policy instrument, yet mobility systems frequently display durable inequalities and core–periphery structures. This study examines whether a regionally bounded program outside Western Europe’s historical academic core functions primarily as an infrastructure of integration or as a mechanism that reproduces stratification. Using openly accessible administrative records from the CEEPUS, the analysis reconstructs a 20-year longitudinal bipartite network of higher education institutions and thematic network agreements (2005/2006–2024/2025). To identify the micro-mechanisms governing network change, the study estimates a bipartite stochastic actor-oriented model in which institutions adjust their memberships over time, while accounting for the creation and discontinuation of thematic networks. The model tests closure mechanism, cumulative advantage, and selection processes based on geopolitical position, research prestige, and institutional type. title: Higher education financing, faculty gender diversity, and STEM graduation outcomes in Europe and Central Asia
abstract: Abstract This study examines how public investment, faculty compensation, and faculty gender diversity relate to system-level STEM graduation rates across 58 countries in Europe and Central Asia, a region underrepresented in comparative higher education research. Using World Bank panel data from 2015 to 2023, we estimate dynamic relationships with a two-step system Generalized Method of Moments model and assess distributional heterogeneity using quantile regression. Results indicate that higher tertiary education expenditure and stronger faculty compensation are associated with higher STEM graduation rates. Moreover, faculty gender diversity positively moderates these relationships, suggesting that more gender-inclusive academic workforces strengthen the extent to which financial investments translate into completion outcomes. The findings underscore the value of integrating financing reforms with equity-oriented staffing strategies to improve STEM attainment and inform higher education policy across diverse national contexts.

title: Ableism, Academic labour, and the myth of meritocracy: reconsidering disability across educational pathways
Status competition in higher education
abstract: Abstract A puzzle for neoliberal reformers in higher education is that regardless of the extent to which systems are remade along neoliberal lines, the outcomes are less transformative than expected. This is because neoliberal competition is articulated by a deeply-ingrained social relation peculiar to higher education: status (prestige) oriented comparison and vertical ordering. Relations between institutions within society are framed by status competition. Status goals permeate the elite sub-sector and shape the middle tiers as the impact of university ranking has shown. Only low status institutions are demand responsive and efficiency driven as imagined by neoliberalism. Yet leading universities have adjusted to meritocratic neoliberalism better than this suggests, drawing on market competition as a legitimating device while building cumulative advantage within it. The neoliberal university market articulates the status order while also being negated by it. The paper focuses on higher education in the Anglosphere. title: Dreaming with the nation: discursive construction and negotiated loyalty in China’s elite basic science programmes
What makes a university public? Publicness in conflict at the Lebanese University, 1959–2019
abstract: Abstract This paper addresses the under-theorised relationship between universities, conflict and the public sphere. Following the history of Lebanon’s only public university over sixty years (1959–2019), through periods of revolution, civil war and neoliberal reconstruction, it explores the question of what makes a university ‘public’ and why this publicness matters in times of conflict and its aftermath. Drawing on interviews with current and former students, faculty and university administrators, alongside newspaper archives, it traces the shifting political significance of the Lebanese University and its making and unmaking as a public sphere. In dialogue with political theory, four conditions of ‘publicness’ emerge, linked to struggles over difference, autonomy, accountability and space/place.

title: Between conflict legacies and global aspirations in conflict-affected middle eastern universities
The leash, the trap, and the labyrinth - supervision, autonomy, and symbolic exclusion in doctoral education in Poland
abstract: Abstract Doctoral education is a critical site for the reproduction of academic power, yet the relational and institutional conditions that shape doctoral candidates’ experiences remain underexplored in non-Anglophone and post-communist contexts. This article examines supervisory and departmental relationships in Polish doctoral education through the lens of power, autonomy, and inclusion, with particular attention to the reconfiguration of these dynamics following the 2018 higher education reform. Drawing on qualitative data from doctoral candidates in law, collected through five focus group interviews and six individual in-depth interviews across both pre- and post-reform cohorts, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, the study identifies three inductively developed metaphors that capture the dominant patterns in participants’ accounts. The leash illuminates the spectrum of supervisory control and autonomy, revealing how both excessive oversight and its absence undermine doctoral candidates’ development. The trap captures the conditional and often ambiguous nature of inclusion within academic communities, where belonging is offered as a benefit but functions as an excha

title: Similar outputs, different positions: convergence and divergence in research activity of public and private universities in EU candidate countries
abstract: Abstract This study draws on neo-institutional theory and the convergence/divergence debate in higher education research to examine whether public and private universities in EU candidate countries converge or diverge in their research activity and collaboration patterns. We analyse Scopus-indexed publication data for 43 universities across Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, North Macedonia and Serbia for the period 2010–2022. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was applied to assess significant differences between the two university groups. The blockmodelling procedure was applied to both non-normalised and normalised co-authorship networks of the universities to estimate the similarity of universities’ collaboration patterns. Our findings reveal that convergence and divergence operate simultaneously but at different analytical layers. At the surface layer of publication output and collaboration indicators, public and private universities are remarkably similar: they do not differ significantly in research productivity per person, share of high-quality output or international collaboration rates. Credential stickiness: how initial educational sorting conditions the value of later credentials in Chinese graduate education
The power of the exemplary: quality teaching in a pedagogical development course in higher education
abstract: Abstract Research points to the importance of a more practice-oriented approach to pedagogical development courses in higher education. In this article, we ask: How are examples of quality teaching expressed by participants in a pedagogical development course and how do they perceive them as meaningful? Employing an ethnographic research design, the study draws on empirical data from seventeen semi-structured interviews, eighteen individual written assignments and fieldnotes from participant observation throughout the course. By using Bildung-centered general didactics and andragogy as a theoretical lens, the results indicate that quality teaching is a matter of (1) selecting the content, (2) exploring the content, and (3) establishing presence and dialogue. These examples are perceived as meaningful because they provide concrete, practice-oriented approaches for restraining and interpreting the content, drawing on prior experiences, and fostering shared and exploratory learning environments. title: Transnational intersectionality: Legal, racial, and national dimensions of institutional marginalization for chinese international students
abstract: Abstract Despite constituting a major population in U.S. higher education, Chinese international students experience institutional marginalization that is often obscured by individual-level deficit narratives. This study adopts transnationalism as an analytic frame to develop an identity-based model, specifying how legal noncitizenship, racialization, and national identity function as institutional mechanisms of exclusion across transnational contexts. It employs Critical Interpretive Synthesis to integrate federal legal and regulatory texts, policy discourse, and a corpus of 58 sources across empirical scholarship, explaining how these dimensions intersect through institutional pathways to co-produce multi-axis vulnerability. The findings theorize a state of “citizenship limbo,” marked by a conditional rights regime and legal exclusion from social welfare supports. From a transnational intersectionality perspective, Chinese international students’ institutional positioning is shaped by the convergence of legal noncitizenship, racialized visibility, and neo-nationalist national interest logics. title: Book Review: Redefining Higher Education: Innovation, Inclusion, and Sustainable Development During Wartime
Seeking balance in higher education in the GenAI era
Illuminating complex student realities of artificial intelligence through an entangled pedagogy framework
abstract: Abstract The emergence of widely available Generative AI (GenAI) in higher education demands nuanced responses that acknowledge the diversity of student contexts, conditions, practices and perspectives. Developing such nuanced responses requires attention to how students themselves experience and negotiate GenAI within the complexity of their everyday study and lives. In this paper, we focus on three participants from a broader set of focus groups to explore their perspectives on GenAI in relation to their studies, identities, and practices, and how contextual and personal factors shape these views. Using Fawns’ (2022) entangled pedagogy framework to guide analysis, we illuminate some complex entanglements that characterise students’ engagement with GenAI. Our analysis reveals how our students’ views were entangled with conceptions of learning, institutional governance, moral positions, and contextual considerations. By focusing on just three participants, we were able to examine the tensions and contradictions in how their relationships with GenAI were shaped in relation to circumstances, purposes, values, practices, identities, institutions, educators, peers, and perceived future

title: Navigating microaggressions in the workplace: experiences of Chinese international academics in England
abstract: Abstract Microaggressions are pervasive within historically white British higher education, but there is little research on Chinese international academics’ experiences and how they navigate microaggressions in their workplace. Drawing on interviews with 41 Chinese academics from four universities in England, this research reveals that 35 participants (85%) experienced or witnessed microaggressions which created a hostile academic environment that undermined their professional standing and cultural identity. The verbal, behavioural, and environmental microaggressions operate through institutional structures that concentrate Chinese academics in junior positions with heavy workloads and deny them voice, credibility, and advancement opportunities. The research participants developed four main response strategies (non-confrontation, active resistance, strategic visibility, and exit planning) to navigate microaggressions, revealing sophisticated negotiations between cultural values, pragmatic assessments of their position, and survival needs. The complex patterns of microaggressions illuminated by this study contribute to better understanding of racial microaggressions in academic sett

title: Beyond casualisation: pathway colleges at the corporate edge of the Australian research university
abstract: Abstract The casualisation of academic work in Australian higher education is increasingly well analysed, yet pathway colleges remain less well understood within that discussion. Existing studies describe pathway educators largely through liminality, unstable professional identity, and racialised or linguistic misrecognition, producing an image of a marginal and precarious workforce. Drawing on publicly available legal and industrial documents, and treating Monash College as the clearest documented case rather than a representative sample, this article explains how that condition is organised through corporate and legal form. Pathway labour is a specific labour form at the corporate edge of the research university — the zone where the university’s legal perimeter meets the subsidiary through which its credentialled but prestige-deficient teaching is externalised. title: Negotiating organizational identity under symbolic autonomy: evidence from regional universities in Kazakhstan
Linguistic unease in multi-domain co-design interactions
abstract: Abstract Co-design is increasingly adopted in Higher Education to support diverse educational innovations. Often framed as inherently collaborative and empowering—promoting inclusivity, agency and collective intelligence—co-design might be underpinned by assumptions of shared understanding and communicative alignment. We problematise these assumptions as multi-domain co-design interactions are dialogical sites prone to linguistic unease, particularly among individuals with heterogenous domains of expertise and specialised linguistic repertoires. Drawing on Linell’s notion of meaning potentials, we conceptualise meaning as created, negotiated and redefined in emergent interactions across participants and contexts, rather than fixed or pre-given. From this perspective, we frame linguistic unease as a potential feature of multi-domain co-design interactions that reveal the limits and possibilities of shared meaning-making. This exploratory study examines how participants experience and navigate linguistic unease in multi-domain co-design interactions. title: Conversion of international academic currency: The impact of tenure-track reform on academic research of Social Sciences and humanities in China
The politics of appointment: reframing leadership studies in higher education governance
Metrics, measures, and the machinery of modern academia
Navigating forcibly displaced learners’ pathways to higher education and beyond: Ukrainian students in French higher education
abstract: Abstract Although there is growing literature on access to and survival in higher education among forcibly displaced migrants, cases of mass displacement across different geographies highlight the need for deeper exploration to understand the role of higher education in mitigating the impact of displacement. The Ukrainian influx to European countries in the aftermath of the country’s full-scale invasion exhibits an entirely different migration structure, both in terms of the origin country and the receiving countries, including the access and survival of Ukrainian forcibly displaced migrants in higher education and the role of higher education in these migrants’ future imaginaries. This study aims to examine the access and experiences of Ukrainian student migrants in French higher education, as well as how they use higher education to construct their desired future. A total of 20 Ukrainian Forcibly Displaced Migrants (UFDMs) were interviewed. title: From education to employment: gendered labour market outcomes across care and non-care fields in Italy and Finland
abstract: Abstract A substantial body of research indicates that graduates’ field of study is a key predictor of the gender wage gap. While previous studies often compare groups based on women’s minority status in a given field, we reframe this by distinguishing between care and non-care fields—defined by their links to stereotypically feminized characteristics and their core care component. Taking the case study of Italy and Finland – representing distinct gender equality contexts, and contrasting welfare state regimes (conservative and Nordic) – we first investigate whether gender gaps in labour market outcomes differ between graduates of care- and non-care related fields of study. Second, adopting a comparative perspective, we further examine whether these gender gaps vary between Italy and Finland. Using administrative data from both countries, which include detailed fields of study classifications, our study supports the gender comparative advantage argument. title: A collectivity of hope to progress anti-racist change in the academy
abstract: Abstract Despair is global white supremacy and antiblackness manifesting itself in our universities. Given this, there remains a question of grasping hope for anti-racist change. Drawing upon interview data with thirty university leaders, the paper contributes to knowledge in the study of race and education by offering up the notion of a collectivity of hope in progressing anti-racist change. I employ an anthropological theoretical model of ethnicity with emphasis on ethnic and racial boundaries to highlight anti-racist work across boundaries to bridge division. This paper demonstrates that this work ties individuals as a collectivity of hope. It is an enchanting thought against a dominant backdrop of race neutrality and color-evasiveness held by many in the academy. As evidenced here, university leaders have agency to challenge the latter. The paper concludes that such change by university leaders may be impossible without a collectivity of hope behind them.

title: Shifting dual promotion pressures and research trade-offs among tenure-track STEM faculty in China: a theoretical framework and empirical evidence
Applications of learning analytics in the study of academic performance in higher education: A meta-review with an educational perspective
abstract: Abstract This meta-review synthesizes evidence from systematic reviews (SRs) examining the application of Learning Analytics (LA) to the study of academic performance in higher education from an educational perspective. Despite growing interest in this area, existing reviews vary considerably in scope and exhibit notable substantive and methodological shortcomings. A comprehensive search strategy, up until May 2025, was conducted across four major databases (Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and PsycINFO), and gray literature. A narrative synthesis was employed to analyze findings from 19 SRs that met the inclusion criteria. The reviewed SRs paid limited attention to key educational aspects, such as instructional contexts, pedagogical aims, disciplinary domains, underlying educational theories, and student learning stages. They were also characterized by critically low methodological quality. Considerable variability was found in how academic performance was conceptualized and operationalized, ranging from broad constructs to clearly defined indicators. Demographic and socioeconomic variables, followed by academic background and performance indicators, were the most frequently examined

title: Academic pathway coherence in public higher education: reframing institutional design in an era of nonlinear student trajectories
Analysing the costs of teaching in universities through structural cost profiling
abstract: Abstract Understanding the structural drivers of teaching cost is a persistent challenge in higher education systems internationally, including in Australia. To extend research on cost heterogeneity and structural cost drivers, we develop and apply a Structural Cost Profiling (SCP) approach, based on Latent Class Analysis (LCA), to analyse 189,811 ‘units of study’ records from 12 Australian universities. Centring on cost per enrolled student, we identify eight distinct cost profiles that capture systematic, multidimensional variation in staffing, enrolment scale, delivery mode and campus location. While the data show significant variation across the dimensions, our analysis demonstrates that cost heterogeneity is not random but structured, with higher average costs per student typically associated with configurations such as (1) regional delivery with small cohorts and labour-intensive postgraduate provision, whereas (2) lower costs emerge from scale-based online delivery models. title: From aspiration to occupation: predictors of STEM career alignment among community college students
Constructing choice, reproducing inequality: a critical assessment of accelerated degrees as a widening participation policy in UK higher education
abstract: Abstract This paper critically examines the UK government’s promotion of accelerated degrees as a widening participation policy in higher education. Although presented as a flexible and efficient route for non-traditional learners, accelerated degrees have seen limited uptake and minimal impact on participation. Drawing on the Social Construction Framework, the paper analyses key policy documents to explore how target learners are discursively constructed and how these constructions shape policy design. It argues that accelerated degrees were advanced through a policy logic centred on choice, flexibility, and efficiency, but one insufficiently attuned to the structural and institutional conditions shaping participation. The paper further shows that institutional responses to accelerated provision were mediated by sectoral norms and differing understandings of legitimate higher education. It concludes that accelerated degrees are better understood not as a failed universal widening participation tool, but as a policy instrument misaligned with many of the learners it purported to support, while retaining more targeted relevance for mature learners. title: Legacy in exile? Refugee professors from Nazi Germany and the reformation of Turkish academia
abstract: Abstract This study reexamines the legacy of refugee professors from Nazi Germany who arrived in Turkey during the 1930s, a formative moment in the reformation of Turkish higher education. Their forced migration coincided with a state-led reform aimed at modernizing the university system along Western lines. The influx of exiled scholars introduced exogenous variation into a developing academic system, creating conditions akin to a natural experiment for examining the long-term effects of academic mobility under political displacement. Using a historical cohort design and documentary review, the study draws on original data for 433 Ph.D. recipients in the Natural and Formal Sciences trained between 1933 and 1969. Archival, bibliographic, and biographical sources are used to reconstruct advisor–student relationships and long-term academic and non-academic outcomes. Multinomial and regression models examine advisor selection and career trajectories across three advisor types: foreign professors, domestic professors with foreign training, and fully domestically trained advisors. Undergraduate students’ understanding and willingness to engage in sustainable development: Insights from Chinese higher education
The ontological design of universities: towards an aspirational decolonial, socio-ecological praxis
abstract: Abstract The essence of the university manifests in its ontological design, which determines future goals and shapes processes and practices across all dimensions of the institution. In this paper, we argue that ontological design matters for universities, for fundamentally transforming institutions, enabling aspirations for decolonisation, and driving a more meaningful contribution to addressing the climate and Nature emergency. Drawing on a study across two South African universities that examined sustainability perceptions and practices in terms of integrated social and ecological justice, the paper interrogates three forms of ontological (re)design in universities – neoliberal policies, a capabilities and well-being orientation, and African ubuntu philosophy. The paper concludes that an ubuntu-capabilitarian ontological design that embeds ecological consciousness and values would steer universities towards an education that fosters pluriversal knowledges, embraces human, spiritual, and non-human interconnection, and embodies ethics of caring, sharing, and repairing. title: ‘I’m just the nuisance crip’: Postqualitative flows of un/belonging for disabled staff and PGR students across UK universities
abstract: Abstract Belonging is recurrently advanced as a significant measure of achievement, retention, and satisfaction among staff and students of higher education. In this article, we examine the politics of un/belonging from the standpoint of disabled academic and professional staff, and PGR students at UK-based institutions of higher education. Drawing on a postqualitative critical disability orientation, the study problematises dominant discourses of belonging that presuppose compliance with an assimilist institutional culture. We present four postqualitative flows (Mazzei, 2013) that conceptualise un/belonging as affective; as divergent from inclusion; as relational; and as agentic and transgressive. Rather than treating the university as a fixed or neutral site to which one might belong, we mobilise subscendence (Morton, 2017) to challenge transcendence and the totalising logic of institutional coherence. Subscendence repositions the university as a porous, contingent assemblage shaped by the masked and embodied experiences of those navigating its norms. The value of this article is its conceptual interrogation of belonging grounded in the empirical accounts of disabled participants

title: Purpose before policy: academic integrity, generative AI, and rhetorical stance
abstract: Abstract The release of ChatGPT in 2022 sparked polarised responses in higher education, from rapid curricular adoption to warnings about academic misconduct and threats to academic integrity. This article argues that whether generative AI (GenAI) use constitutes misconduct depends on a prior question: what is the university’s purpose? We contend that (apparent) rising GenAI-related misconduct cases reflect structural incoherence in the neo-liberal university, where technological enthusiasm, corporate influence, and policy enforcement often conflict. Such misalignment produces moral and institutional ambiguity, leaving students accountable for behaviours implicitly shaped by the institution itself. Drawing on an historical and rhetorical account of the Anglo-American university model, we analyse mission statements from leading university networks to reveal gaps between how institutional ideals are communicated versus how they are implemented. We conclude that universities cannot credibly enforce integrity standards in the age of AI without first ensuring coherence between their stated missions, pedagogical practices, and approaches to emerging technologies.

title: Widening access, closing minds? The paradox of career aspiration and graduate employability in South Africa
abstract: Abstract In the global context of higher education massification and the shifting demands of the labour market, understanding the drivers of student career aspirations is critical. This study interrogates the “graduateness paradox” in South Africa—where expanded access has not yet yielded equitable employment outcomes—by moving beyond simplistic “skills gap” narratives. Employing Pierre Bourdieu’s theories of habitus, capital, and field, we analyse the real-time formation of professional ambition among current students. Drawing on a cross-sectional survey of N = 1,149 students across four diverse South African universities, we utilised hierarchical multiple regression to test the influence of employability skills, institutional support (employability stimulating factors), confidence, and work experience on career aspirations. Quantifying inequality, qualifying experiences: socioeconomic status and employment outcomes among Australian doctoral graduates
abstract: Abstract Despite expanded access to higher education in Australia, questions remain regarding whether socioeconomic background continues to influence post-graduation outcomes at the doctoral level. This study examines whether employment and earnings disparities persist among doctoral graduates from low-, medium-, and high-socioeconomic status (SES) backgrounds. Adopting a multi-layered approach, this study complements quantitative analyses of national Graduate Outcomes Survey data (GOS, 2016–2023) and longitudinal datasets (GOS-L, 2019–2023) with narrative case studies of two low-SES doctoral graduates who have sustained academic careers within Australian universities. Quantitative findings reveal that while employment outcomes were largely comparable across SES groups, low-SES graduates reported marginally lower median salaries six months after graduation.
